Diastolic blood pressure in adults aged 30 and over in Bharatpur, Nepal

Dataset 3: Nepal hypertension and cardiovascular risk-factor survey

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

This is a community-based cross-sectional survey of adults aged 30 years and over living in Bharatpur, Chitwan district, Nepal, designed to estimate the prevalence of hypertension and describe its behavioural and anthropometric correlates (Dhungana and colleagues, PLOS ONE 2016, e0185806). Blood pressure was measured twice with a digital device and averaged, and the WHO STEPS instrument was used for tobacco, alcohol, diet and physical activity, with height and weight measured directly. Diastolic pressure is analysed separately from systolic here because the two behave differently with age – diastolic pressure plateaus and then falls in later life as arteries stiffen, whereas systolic pressure keeps rising – so the same predictor set can give a noticeably different picture.

Aim. Among adults aged 30 and over in Bharatpur, we examined which of sex, age band, education, occupation, poverty, smoking, smokeless tobacco, alcohol, fruit and vegetable intake, salt intake, physical activity, family history of hypertension and body mass index are independently associated with mean diastolic blood pressure, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. A cross-sectional survey of 1159 adults aged 30 years and over resident in Bharatpur Municipality, Chitwan, Nepal. The source study used multistage cluster sampling: four wards were selected at random and approximately 300 participants enrolled in each, with the sample size calculation assuming a design effect of 1.5. The ward identifier is absent from this extract, with direct consequences for the standard errors (see Limitations). Each row is one participant.

Variables. The outcome is diastolic_bp, the mean of two diastolic readings in mmHg. Predictors are sex (reference Female); age band in years (reference 30-39; age was recorded only in four bands, so a per-year effect cannot be estimated); education (reference None or informal); main occupation (reference Household work); family income per head below the poverty line (reference No); smoking status (reference Never); current smokeless tobacco use (reference No); any alcohol in the last month (reference No); fruit and vegetable servings per day; estimated salt intake in g/day; physical activity level (reference Moderate or high); family history of hypertension (reference No); and body mass index in kg/m2.

Systolic pressure is deliberately not a predictor. It is measured on the same occasion, on the same arm, from the same physiology, and correlates with diastolic at r = 0.79; including it would produce a large, meaningless coefficient and drive every other estimate to zero. For the same reason hypertension, bp_awareness and antihypertensive_drug are excluded: hypertension is defined as raised measured pressure or current treatment, so it is a function of the outcome, and the other two are consequences of having been found hypertensive in the past. Two further pairs measure the same construct twice and only one member of each may enter: physical_activity is a deterministic cut of mets_min_per_week at 600 MET-minutes per week (the “Low” group spans 0-600, “Moderate or high” spans 620-29,260) and the categorical version is used because it is the WHO STEPS classification reported in the source paper; and cigarettes_per_week is zero for every never-smoker, so smoking_status is used instead because it distinguishes former from never smokers.

Statistical analysis. Linear regression via lm(), justified because the outcome is continuous. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Significance threshold 0.05; estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals. Assumptions were checked with performance::check_model(), and because non-constant error variance was flagged, HC3 heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors are reported alongside the ordinary ones. Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary, performance and sandwich.

Missing data. Complete-case analysis: 1159 of 1159 rows were analysed (0 dropped). Every variable in this file is 100% complete, so listwise deletion removes no rows at all. There is no missing-data story here: no imputation is required and complete-case selection bias cannot arise.

Mean diastolic pressure was 80.9 mmHg (SD 12.4), a much narrower distribution than the systolic one. The sample is 71.1% female, 35.8% are classified as physically inactive, and 131 participants (11.3%) were on antihypertensive medication when measured. Their mean diastolic pressure was 87.4 mmHg against 80 mmHg in the untreated – a gap of 7.4 mmHg that exists despite treatment and therefore understates the underlying difference.

Exploratory figure

Figure 2. Diastolic blood pressure by age band, separately for participants taking and not taking antihypertensive medication. The dashed line marks the 90 mmHg threshold.

Diastolic pressure rises across the age bands but far less steeply than systolic does – mean values run 77.9, 81, 82.5, 83.7 mmHg against roughly 115 to 134 mmHg for systolic – and the rise is mostly between the two youngest bands. At every age the treated participants sit higher than the untreated (means around 87-88 mmHg regardless of age), and the treated boxes are wider, which is what one expects when a heterogeneous group of people on different drugs at different doses is compared with an untreated group; note also that only 11 of the 30-39 band are treated, so that box rests on very few people.

Body mass index is again the clearest continuous predictor: each additional kg/m2 is associated with a 0.86 mmHg higher diastolic pressure (95% CI 0.7 to 1.02, p < 0.001), which across the interquartile range of BMI in this sample amounts to roughly 4.6 mmHg. The age gradient is much shallower than for systolic pressure – participants aged 60 or more average 5.9 mmHg above the 30-39 band (95% CI 3.9 to 7.8), against about 21 mmHg for systolic – which is the expected physiology. Men average 4.2 mmHg above women (95% CI 2.7 to 5.8), drinkers 5.1 mmHg above non-drinkers, former smokers 7.2 mmHg above never-smokers, and smokeless tobacco users 3.7 mmHg above non-users. Salt intake is once more flat (-0.09 mmHg per g/day, 95% CI -0.4 to 0.23).

Why adjustment is needed

Almost every crude estimate above is contaminated by two variables in this dataset. Age band is the first. It is associated with diastolic pressure and simultaneously with practically every exposure here: former smokers are concentrated in the older bands (quitting is an older person’s behaviour), 209 of the 263 participants aged 60 or more have no or informal schooling against 114 of 383 among the 30-39 year olds, and occupation shifts from paid employment towards household work and unemployment with age. A crude coefficient for education or occupation therefore contains an age effect. Sex is the second and is even starker here, because tobacco and alcohol in this population are overwhelmingly male behaviours: 35% of men are current smokers against 11% of women, and men have higher diastolic pressure regardless. The crude smokeless tobacco and alcohol coefficients are therefore partly measuring maleness. Body mass index is the third: it is the strongest single predictor of diastolic pressure in the file and it varies systematically across occupation, poverty and smoking groups (smokers are leaner), so omitting it lets those coefficients absorb an adiposity effect – sometimes in the wrong direction. Mutual adjustment is what separates these three overlapping gradients from the behaviours of interest.

The model explains 19.2% of the variance in diastolic pressure (adjusted R-squared 0.178), a little better than the corresponding systolic model but still leaving the great majority unexplained. With 1159 observations and 21 parameters there are 55.2 observations per parameter, so overfitting is not a concern. Conditional on the other twelve predictors, each additional kg/m2 of BMI is associated with a 0.94 mmHg higher diastolic pressure (95% CI 0.78 to 1.1); participants aged 60 or more average 5.2 mmHg above the 30-39 band (95% CI 3.1 to 7.3); men average 2.2 mmHg above women (95% CI 0.2 to 4.1, p = 0.029); and recent drinkers average 2.8 mmHg above non-drinkers (95% CI 0.6 to 4.9).

As in the systolic model, the smoking coefficients are the wrong way round for a causal reading: former smokers are 5 mmHg above never-smokers (95% CI 3.1 to 6.9) while current smokers are indistinguishable from never-smokers (0.3 mmHg, 95% CI -1.7 to 2.3). The natural explanation is reverse causation: in a cross-sectional survey “former smoker” partly identifies people who quit after being told they had a cardiovascular problem. Salt intake remains null (0.08 mmHg per g/day, 95% CI -0.21 to 0.37), as does family history (-0.2 mmHg).

Adjusted estimates (mmHg, 95% CI)
All n = 1159; untreated n = 1028
Term All participants Untreated only
BMI (per kg/m2) 0.94 (0.78 to 1.10) 0.97 (0.80 to 1.14)
Age 60+ vs 30-39 5.22 (3.13 to 7.31) 4.98 (2.73 to 7.24)
Male vs female 2.15 (0.22 to 4.09) 2.57 (0.51 to 4.62)
Alcohol last month 2.78 (0.62 to 4.95) 3.06 (0.72 to 5.40)

131 participants were taking medication whose entire purpose is to lower the quantity being measured, so diastolic_bp in this file is a partly treated outcome. Refitting in the 1028 untreated participants moves the estimates very little: BMI goes from 0.94 to 0.97 mmHg per kg/m2 and the oldest-band contrast from 5.2 to 5 mmHg. The stability is reassuring but should not be over-read: treatment is concentrated in the older and heavier participants and pulls their readings down, so the full-sample coefficients for age and BMI are attenuated rather than inflated. Restricting to the untreated is also not a clean fix, because being untreated is itself a consequence of blood pressure, so this restriction trades treatment bias for selection bias. Both fits are shown for that reason.

Several estimates move a long way, all toward the null. Alcohol in the last month falls from 5.1 mmHg crude (95% CI 3.1 to 7, p < 0.001) to 2.8 mmHg adjusted (95% CI 0.6 to 4.9, p = 0.012), a 45% reduction: roughly half the crude alcohol association is being male and being older. Smokeless tobacco goes from 3.7 mmHg crude (p <0.001) to 1.5 mmHg adjusted (p = 0.23) and loses significance entirely – the same confounding by sex and age. Low physical activity goes from 2 mmHg (p = 0.008) to 0.68 mmHg (p = 0.34), also losing significance, because inactivity in this sample is largely a marker of being old and heavy. Being in paid employment rather than doing household work moves from 2.9 mmHg (p = 0.001) to 1.5 mmHg (p = 0.1) – a sex effect in disguise, since paid employment here is disproportionately male. Sex itself roughly halves, from 4.2 to 2.2 mmHg, and only barely stays significant.

Two estimates barely move, and one of them moves away from the null. Age 60 or more goes from 5.9 to 5.2 mmHg, a shift of under 15%, as expected for a variable that nothing else in the model can confound. BMI goes from 0.86 to 0.94 mmHg per kg/m2 – slightly larger after adjustment, which happens because BMI is negatively associated with smoking and with the older age bands, so the crude estimate was being pulled down by those. This is negative confounding rather than mediation or collinearity; the maximum variance inflation factor in the model is 1.83, so no coefficient is unstable.

salt_g_per_day 0.079 0.149 0.144 -0.20 to 0.36 0.582

The posterior-predictive check shows the model reproducing the bulk of the diastolic distribution but missing the digit-preference spikes at 70, 80 and 90 mmHg that are visible in the raw data: readings were recorded to the nearest whole number by a human operator and cluster on multiples of ten, which no continuous model can reproduce. The linearity panel is close to flat. The homogeneity of variance panel shows a mild fan, and check_heteroscedasticity() flags it at p 0.05 – borderline rather than gross, but flagged. As heteroscedasticity biases standard errors and not coefficients, HC3 robust standard errors are reported above; they are almost identical to the OLS ones (BMI 0.082 versus 0.082), so no substantive conclusion changes, but the robust version is the one to quote. Collinearity is not an issue: maximum VIF 1.83, which is only achievable because systolic_bp, mets_min_per_week and cigarettes_per_week were kept out. Influential observations shows no point beyond the Cook’s distance contour. Normality of residuals shows mild departure at both tails, partly from the digit preference; with 1159 observations this does not threaten the coefficient estimates.

Discussion

Diastolic blood pressure in these Bharatpur adults is driven by body mass index and, more weakly than systolic pressure, by age. Each kg/m2 of BMI corresponds to about 0.94 mmHg, so the difference between a BMI of 22 and 28 is roughly 5.6 mmHg; being 60 or over rather than in one’s thirties adds about 5 mmHg. Alcohol retains a modest independent association of 2.8 mmHg. Everything else – salt, physical activity, fruit and vegetables, family history, poverty, education, smokeless tobacco – is null once age, sex and BMI are accounted for. Practically, this is another argument that weight is the single actionable target in this population, and a warning that the crude lifestyle associations that make attractive headlines here are mostly demographic confounding.

Limitations. The most serious problem is treatment bias in the outcome. 131 participants (11.3%) were on antihypertensive medication when measured, so what this file records is diastolic pressure as currently treated, and because treatment is concentrated in those with the highest underlying pressure, coefficients for any risk factor that also predicts treatment are attenuated by an unknown amount. The sensitivity analysis bounds this rather than removing it. Second, the cluster sampling cannot be modelled: only four wards were randomly selected and about 300 participants enrolled in each, with a design effect of 1.5 assumed in the sample size calculation, but no ward identifier exists in this extract. The confidence intervals reported above are therefore too narrow – plausibly by around 20% – and no mixed or survey-weighted model can repair that. Four clusters also make any claim of representativeness of Nepal, or even of Bharatpur as a whole, unsupportable. Third, age is available only in four bands, so no per-year slope is estimable and the top band is open-ended. Fourth, this is cross-sectional, so associations are not causal effects, and the former-smoker coefficient is a live demonstration of reverse causation. Fifth, diastolic readings show clear terminal-digit preference at multiples of ten, which adds measurement noise and slightly distorts the residual distribution. Sixth, salt intake is estimated rather than measured by 24-hour urinary sodium, so its null association may be measurement error rather than biology. Seventh, adjusted R-squared is only 0.178. On the credit side, the file has no missing data at all: all 1159 rows are complete on all 21 variables.

Future work. Obtain the ward identifier and refit with a random intercept for ward; and repeat the analysis on a bias-corrected outcome that adds a fixed 5-10 mmHg diastolic offset to treated participants.

Feasibility notes

Not part of a student report.

  • Works, with the same large caveat as systolic. Continuous outcome, 100% complete data, 1159 rows over 21 parameters, max VIF 1.83, adjusted R-squared 0.178, and genuine confounding that visibly moves the alcohol, smokeless tobacco, occupation and physical activity coefficients.
  • This file is very close to systolic_bp.Rmd. If both are offered to students, expect near-identical reports. The one genuinely different finding is the much shallower age gradient (5.2 mmHg here versus about 16 mmHg for systolic), which is real physiology and worth making the students explain. Otherwise consider offering only one of the two.
  • The treatment trap applies identically. Treated mean diastolic 87.4 versus 80 mmHg untreated. A student who adjusts for antihypertensive_drug is adjusting for a consequence of the outcome.
  • Forbidden predictors. systolic_bp (r = 0.79 with the outcome), hypertension (deterministic function of the outcome), bp_awareness and antihypertensive_drug.
  • Deterministic twins. physical_activity is exactly mets_min_per_week <= 600; cigarettes_per_week is zero for all never-smokers. Never use both members of either pair.
  • Heteroscedasticity is flagged but only just (p 0.05), which makes this a slightly awkward teaching example: a student re-running it after any change to the predictor set may see it pass. HC3 standard errors change nothing here.
  • Digit preference. Diastolic values pile up on 70/80/90. Harmless for regression but it makes the QQ and posterior-predictive panels look worse than the model deserves, and students will over-interpret that.
  • No ward identifier, so the assumed design effect of 1.5 cannot be honoured; standard errors are too narrow throughout.
  • Age in bands only, so no “mmHg per year” figure is available.
